learningPath.title: Connected Learning
learningPath.description: The connected learning path. Competencies demonstrated in one course are reused by later courses rather than duplicated.

course.title: Networking Foundations
course.description: Start from nothing and build a working mental model of how two machines reach each other. You will meet the devices a network is made of, watch traffic move inside one network, learn the two identities a machine carries, work out the decision every machine makes about where to send something, follow a message across a boundary and back, test whether it truly arrived, and repair a simple failure. Before this course you need only the ability to operate a computer, use a keyboard and mouse, navigate a web application, and compare two numbers. No networking vocabulary is assumed: every term you need is introduced here, after you have already seen the behavior it names.

modules.title: One Network
modules.description: What a network is made of, and how something gets from one machine to another when both are on the same network. Everything here happens inside a single network; boundaries come later.

modules.title: Addresses and Boundaries
modules.description: The second identity a machine carries, and the decision it makes with it: is what I am trying to reach on my own network, or somewhere else? This is the question the rest of the course depends on.

modules.title: Reaching Another Network
modules.description: What a machine does when the answer is "somewhere else": who it hands the message to, what that device does with it, and what the whole trip looks like from one end to the other.

modules.title: Prove It and Fix It
modules.description: Establishing whether something genuinely works rather than appears to, and what to do when it does not. The failure here is bounded and visible; finding a fault you were not shown belongs to a later course.

missions.title: Mission 1 — Follow a print request across a network
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read, count, and compare two numbers. Nothing else.

A user at PC-A sends a document to the network printer. In this mission, you follow that print request across a small office network and predict which device receives it next.

You begin with the journey. The network is already connected, so your task is to trace the request from PC-A to the Printer and observe which devices and links it uses.

After the journey, you name what you just worked with: hosts, interfaces and ports, the switch that carries the request across the local network, the router at the edge, and the topology that shows how the devices connect.

This mission does not teach how Switch-1 decides which port to use. That question is left for Mission 2.

Nothing is configured or changed here. You are learning to read a network before you are asked to alter one.

content.title: Follow a print request across a network
paragraphs: A small office network has two computers, a shared printer, a switch, and a router at the edge. Someone at PC-A sends a document to the network printer.
Your job: follow that print request from PC-A to the Printer and identify the devices it passes through along the way.
Start with the journey. Watch where the print request goes first and which connections it uses. Afterward, we will name the devices and connections you just worked with.
You will not configure anything in this mission. Select a device whenever you want to inspect what it is and what it connects to.

content.caption: Follow the print request from PC-A to the Printer.
content.textEquivalent: This activity shows five devices: PC-A, PC-B, the Printer, Switch-1, and Router-1. PC-A, PC-B, and the Printer each connect to Switch-1. Router-1 also connects to Switch-1 and has another connection leading beyond this local network. PC-A is sending a print request to the Printer. Use the connections in the topology to predict which device receives the print request first. You can select any device to inspect what it connects to.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the computer a person is working at, and it is where this print request begins. It has one network connection, and that connection runs to Switch-1.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is a second computer on this local network, connected to Switch-1 the same way PC-A is. It is here because a network is shared: several machines connect to the same switch, each on a connection of its own. This print request came from PC-A, so PC-B plays no part in it.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is the shared network printer, and it is what this print request is for. It is a host like PC-A and PC-B, with a connection into Switch-1 of its own, which is what lets any computer on this network send it work.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 is the device in the middle of this local network. PC-A, PC-B, the Printer and Router-1 each connect to a port on it, so anything one of them sends arrives at Switch-1 first. Mission 2 explains how Switch-1 decides which port to send it out of.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 sits at the edge of this local network, with one port facing Switch-1 and one port leading away. It is the way out when a machine here needs to reach something that is not on this network. This print request does not use Router-1, because PC-A and the Printer are both on this local network. Mission 5 explains why a computer sends traffic to a router when what it wants is somewhere else.

stages.narration: The print request is now leaving PC-A on the link toward Switch-1.

prediction.prompt: PC-A sends the print request toward the Printer. Which device receives the print request first?
options: Switch-1
Printer
Router-1
prediction.explanation: PC-A has one network connection, and that connection leads to Switch-1 port 1. The print request reaches Switch-1 before it can reach the Printer.

stages.narration: The print request reaches Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 carries the request toward the Printer through port 3.
The print request reaches the Printer through the link from Switch-1 port 3. The Printer accepts the print job.

confirmation.narration: Delivered. The print request reached the Printer.
confirmation.summary:
PC-A sent the request, Switch-1 carried it across the local network, and the Printer received it.

You have now followed one print request across a small network. Next, you will name the devices and connections you just used.

content.title: What is a host?
paragraphs: A host is a device that sends or receives network traffic for itself. Computers, servers, phones, and network printers can all be hosts.
PC-A sent the print request, and the Printer received it, so both acted as hosts in the journey you just followed.
The Printer is drawn with a printer icon so you can recognize its job. For this lesson, the important point is that it is also connected to the network and can receive traffic addressed to it.

content.title: Network connections
paragraphs: PC-A did not send the print request simply because the Printer was nearby. PC-A has a specific connection to the network. The point where a device connects to a network is called an interface.

Switch-1 has several physical connection points called ports. Port 1 connects to PC-A, and port 3 connects to the Printer. Network-device software also represents these connections as interfaces, so you will encounter both terms as you begin working with device commands.
A connection between two network interfaces is called a link. In this topology, PC-A has one link, and that link connects PC-A to Switch-1.

content.title: Switches and routers
paragraphs: Not every device in the topology is a host. Some network devices primarily move traffic between other devices. In the journey you just followed, Switch-1 carried the print request between PC-A and the Printer.

In this topology, PC-A, PC-B, and the Printer each connect to Switch-1 instead of connecting directly to one another. A switch connects devices within a local network and forwards traffic between its ports. This device is Switch-1.

Router-1 is connected to this local network and also to another network beyond it. A router connects different networks and can forward traffic between them. The print request you followed stayed inside the local network, so it did not use Router-1.

content.title: Reading the topology
paragraphs: The drawing you used is a network topology. A topology shows how network devices and links are arranged and connected.

A topology is not a floor plan. Devices drawn close together may be in different rooms, and a short line may represent a link that spans a much greater physical distance. Read the diagram for network relationships, not room-to-room distance.
You can now look at a small topology, identify the hosts, switch, and router, identify the links between them, and trace the path traffic must take between two hosts.

content.title: Try it on a different network
content.framing: This network uses different devices, but the same ideas still apply. Use the topology to answer each question.

topology.textEquivalent: Laptop-A connects to Switch-2. Server-A connects to Switch-2. Router-2 connects to Switch-2. Router-2 also connects to another network.

questions.prompt: Which two devices are hosts in this topology?
questions.explanation: Laptop-A and Server-A send or receive network traffic for themselves, so both are hosts.

questions.prompt: Which device carries traffic between Laptop-A and Server-A on this local network?
questions.explanation: Both hosts connect to Switch-2, so traffic between them passes through the switch.

questions.prompt: Which device connects this local network to another network?
questions.explanation: Router-2 has a connection to this network and another connection leading beyond it, so it connects different networks.

questions.prompt: Laptop-A sends traffic to Server-A. Which device does that traffic reach first?
questions.explanation: Laptop-A's link connects to Switch-2, so the traffic reaches Switch-2 before it can reach Server-A.

paragraphs: You can now identify the main devices and connections in a small network and follow traffic between two hosts. The next question is how a switch decides which port to use. Mission 2 answers that.

missions.title: Mission 2 — Inside one network: how a switch delivers
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a small network and name its devices and connections (Mission 1).

PC-A and PC-B share one local network through Switch-1. PC-A sends a local-network delivery toward PC-B. You will follow the first delivery, a reply, and a later delivery between the same two hosts and compare what changes.

Do not try to name the mechanism yet. First watch what Switch-1 can see, what the network does, and what information becomes available as traffic arrives.

By the end you will be able to explain how a switch uses learned local information to deliver traffic, read the interface identity used for that local delivery, and distinguish expected switching behavior from a fault.

content.title: One local delivery, two machines
paragraphs: PC-A and PC-B are on the same local network, each connected to Switch-1. Someone at PC-A sends data to a colleague at PC-B.
Your job: follow one local-network delivery from PC-A toward PC-B, then compare it with a later delivery between the same two hosts.
PC-A already has the local interface identity it needs for PC-B. How PC-A learned that identity comes later; for this mission, take that starting fact as given.
Watch Switch-1 and compare the state you can observe before each delivery. Name the mechanism only after you have seen it.

content.caption: An instructional walkthrough of the local deliveries on one network. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A small local network contains PC-A, PC-B, a Printer, and Switch-1. PC-A connects to Switch-1 port 1, PC-B to port 2, and the Printer to port 3. PC-A is sending a local-network delivery intended for PC-B. Each host interface has a local hardware address visible in the inspector. Use the activity to observe what Switch-1 does on the first delivery, what information becomes available from traffic it receives, what changes after PC-B sends a reply, and what happens on a later delivery. The outcomes are revealed as you progress through the activity.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the host where this activity begins. It connects to Switch-1 port 1.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is the intended destination for the first local-network delivery. It connects to Switch-1 port 2.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is another host on this local network. It connects to Switch-1 port 3, but it is not the intended destination.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 connects all three hosts. Select it as the activity progresses to inspect the state the lesson has revealed so far.

stages.action: sending a local-network delivery to PC-B
stages.narration: PC-A puts one local-network delivery onto its connection toward Switch-1. The delivery is intended for PC-B.
stages.decision: PC-A sends using the local interface identity it already has for PC-B. How that identity was discovered is outside this mission.

stages.action: receiving the delivery and choosing outgoing connections
stages.narration: The delivery reaches Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 has no recorded location for PC-B, so it sends a copy through port 2 and port 3. It does not send a copy back out port 1.
stages.decision: When the destination is not in its recorded locations, Switch-1 uses every other port so the delivery can reach whichever port leads to PC-B.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has no recorded location for PC-B. What do you think it does with this delivery?
options: Sends it through port 2 only
Sends a copy through port 2 and port 3
Sends it back through port 1 and waits

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why can Switch-1 record PC-A on port 1 after this arrival?
options: Because the delivery arrived on port 1 with PC-A as its source
Because PC-B is connected to port 2
Because the Printer ignored its copy
knowledgeChecks.correctOption: Because the delivery arrived on port 1 with PC-A as its source
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A switch learns from the source of traffic it receives. This delivery arrived on port 1 from PC-A, so the arrival supports the PC-A-to-port-1 entry.

stages.narration: One copy reaches PC-B on port 2 and is accepted because the delivery is intended for PC-B. At the same time, the other copy reaches the Printer on port 3. The Printer sees that the delivery is not intended for it and does not accept it.
stages.decision: Nothing is broken. Switch-1 had no recorded location for PC-B, so both other ports carried a copy. Only the intended destination accepts the delivery.

facts.label: Copy arrived
facts.value: Not accepted — the delivery is intended for PC-B

stages.narration: PC-B replies. The reply reaches Switch-1 on port 2.
stages.decision: This arrival shows Switch-1 that traffic sourced by PC-B is arriving through port 2, so Switch-1 records PC-B on port 2.

stages.narration: Switch-1 already has a recorded location for PC-A, so the reply leaves only through port 1 and reaches PC-A. The Printer's port is not used for this reply.
stages.decision: The destination is already in the recorded locations, so Switch-1 can use the single recorded port.

stages.action: sending another local-network delivery to PC-B
stages.narration: A little later, PC-A sends another local-network delivery to PC-B. The hosts and links are unchanged.
stages.decision: Before the delivery moves through Switch-1, compare what Switch-1 has recorded with what it had at the start.

stages.narration: The delivery reaches Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 already has PC-B recorded on port 2, so it sends the delivery only through port 2. Port 3 remains unused.
stages.decision: This time the destination has a recorded location, so one outgoing port is enough.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 now has PC-B recorded on port 2. What will it do with this delivery?
options: Send a copy through port 2 and port 3
Send it through port 2 only
Send it back through port 1
prediction.explanation: PC-B is already recorded on port 2, so Switch-1 can send this delivery through that port without using the Printer's port.

stages.narration: The delivery reaches PC-B through port 2. The Printer does not receive a copy this time.
stages.decision: Compare the two deliveries: the topology did not change. What changed was the location information Switch-1 had learned from earlier traffic.

confirmation.narration: Delivered. The later delivery reached PC-B without using the Printer's port.
confirmation.summary: On the first delivery, Switch-1 had no recorded location for PC-B and used both other ports. From incoming traffic, it learned PC-A on port 1 and then PC-B on port 2 when PC-B replied. On the later delivery, the recorded location for PC-B let Switch-1 use port 2 only. Next, you will name the local identities and table entries you just used.

content.title: What you just watched
paragraphs: The first time, Switch-1 had no recorded location for PC-B. Sending copies out every other port in that situation is called flooding.
Flooding is expected behavior when the destination is not in the switch's recorded locations. The switch does not send the copy back through the port where the traffic arrived.

At the same time, a switch can learn from the source of incoming traffic. PC-A's delivery arrived on port 1, so Switch-1 could record PC-A on port 1. PC-B's reply arrived on port 2, so Switch-1 could record PC-B on port 2.
The order matters. A switch learns a source from traffic that actually arrives. It does not learn where a quiet destination is merely because another host is trying to reach it.
Once PC-B had sent traffic of its own, Switch-1 had enough local information to use port 2 for the later delivery instead of flooding it.

content.title: The identity on an interface
paragraphs: The local interface identity you saw in the inspector is called a MAC address. A switch reads source and destination MAC addresses while handling local Ethernet traffic.
A MAC address belongs to a network interface rather than to the whole machine. A device with more than one network interface can therefore have more than one MAC address.

Many physical interfaces are given a MAC address by their manufacturer, but a MAC address is not an immutable hardware serial number. Software and virtual interfaces can use locally administered or changed MAC addresses. For this mission, the important fact is the current MAC address on the interface.

The record you watched Switch-1 build is called a MAC address table. Each learned entry associates a source MAC address with the port where the switch most recently saw traffic from that source. In this simple topology, one host is directly connected to each port, so the walkthrough used device names for readability. A real switch can learn more than one MAC address through the same port.

content.caption: Field excerpt from ip link show eth0. Real output includes interface state and additional fields around this value; this excerpt preserves only the link/ether field and MAC address used in this mission.

content.title: The unit that moved
paragraphs: The switch does not forward an entire application file as one indivisible object. The local-network delivery you followed represents one Ethernet frame carrying data for the communication.
A frame carries source and destination MAC addresses and moves across a local Ethernet link from interface to interface.
A file transfer normally requires many frames. This mission follows one representative frame so you can reason about the switch's local delivery decision without adding the higher-layer details yet.
When traffic must leave this local network, another unit has a different job. You will meet that later, after you have a reason to use it.

content.title: Looks wrong, works as designed
paragraphs: The Printer receiving a copy during the first delivery did not mean the network was broken. It was an expected consequence of flooding while Switch-1 lacked a destination entry for PC-B.
Troubleshooting starts by separating an observation from a conclusion. Ask what state the device had, then ask whether the behavior is consistent with that state.
You will reuse that habit when later missions introduce behavior that really is a fault.

content.title: Try it on a different switch
content.framing: A different office uses Switch-2 with two workstations and a camera. Use the topology and the MAC-table state stated in each question. Nothing here requires configuration.

topology.textEquivalent: Workstation-A connects to Switch-2 port 1. Workstation-B connects to Switch-2 port 2. The Camera connects to Switch-2 port 3.

questions.prompt: Switch-2 has no MAC-table entry for Workstation-B. A frame from Workstation-A arrives on port 1 for Workstation-B. Which ports should carry copies next?
questions.explanation: Because Workstation-B is not in the table, Switch-2 floods the frame through the other ports. It does not send the frame back out the ingress port 1.

questions.prompt: From that same arrival on port 1, which entry can Switch-2 learn immediately?

options.text: None until an administrator configures the switch

questions.explanation: A switch learns from the source MAC address of traffic it receives. The frame arrived on port 1 from Workstation-A, so Switch-2 can learn Workstation-A on port 1.

questions.prompt: The Camera receives a copy of that first frame, but the destination MAC address belongs to Workstation-B. What does the Camera receiving the copy establish?

options.text: This can be expected during flooding and does not by itself establish a fault
The Camera's MAC address must have changed

questions.explanation: An unknown destination can cause the switch to flood the frame through the other ports. An unintended host seeing that copy is therefore not enough by itself to establish a fault.

questions.prompt: Later, after Workstation-B sends a reply, Switch-2 has learned Workstation-B on port 2. Workstation-A sends another frame to Workstation-B. Which port should Switch-2 use?
questions.explanation: Workstation-B is now a known destination on port 2, so Switch-2 can forward the frame through port 2 without flooding it to the Camera.

content.title: What comes next
paragraphs: You can now explain why a switch floods when a destination MAC address is not yet in its table, how it learns source MAC locations from arriving frames, and why later traffic can use a single learned port.
Mission 3 adds a second kind of interface identity. You will read it from a host and compare what it tells you with the local MAC identity you used here.

missions.title: Mission 3 — IPv4 addresses: the second identity
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: explain how a switch uses MAC addresses and learned port mappings for local delivery (Mission 2).

Every interface you have looked at already has a MAC address used for local Ethernet delivery. So why does the same interface also need an IPv4 address?

A MAC address identifies an interface for local Ethernet delivery, but it is not the address this course will use to organize machines into IP networks. An IPv4 address is assigned to the interface, is written as four decimal numbers separated by dots, and can be chosen to reflect which IP network the interface belongs to.

You will look at displayed machine output and find the IPv4 address beside the interface that holds it. Reading the machine's own report is how you confirm its current state instead of relying on a diagram or memory.

This mission does not yet teach how the host uses the IPv4 address to decide whether another address is local or remote. That decision needs the number after the slash, and it is the next mission.

Addresses can be configured manually or assigned automatically. This course uses controlled values so you can see exactly what is where. Names such as hostnames are a separate system and are not needed for this exercise.

By the end you will be able to read a machine's IPv4 address from displayed output, say which interface holds it, and explain how its job differs from the MAC address you used in Mission 2.

content.title: One connection, two identities
paragraphs: A machine is on the network and working, and you have been asked to identify it — to say which machine it is and where it sits.
Your job: read what PC-A reports about itself, and find the identity that answers the second half of that question.
In Mission 2 you read PC-A's MAC address from its interface and watched Switch-1 learn that source MAC on port 1. That address mattered for local Ethernet delivery.
But the MAC address does not tell you which IP network the interface belongs to. The interface needs a different kind of address for that job.
Inside the local Ethernet network, Switch-1 could deliver using learned MAC-to-port entries. The next questions need a different kind of address.
So the interface already has a MAC address. Why does it also need an IP address? Do not take the answer from this page — look at what the machine reports about itself.

content.caption: PC-A, reporting on the connection you already know by name. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Real output carries several more lines and several more fields than this; two lines are shown, and you met one of them in Mission 2. Before you read on: find the line you have not seen before, and say which connection is holding it.

content.title: The second identity
paragraphs: The line you had not seen before begins with inet, and the interface holding it is eth0 — the same interface whose MAC address you read in Mission 2. One interface can carry both at once. Neither replaces the other.
The four numbers separated by dots, 192.168.1.10, are an IPv4 address. An IPv4 address is assigned to an interface, can be changed, and can be chosen as part of an addressing plan.

Hold the two jobs apart. The MAC address is used for local Ethernet delivery. The IPv4 address is the interface's assigned IP address; with the number after the slash that you will learn next, it helps the host reason about which IP network an address belongs to.
Both addresses can exist on the same interface and both can be read from the machine's own state. They answer different networking questions.

content.caption: A different machine on the same network, reporting the same way. This is displayed output again — nothing here offers to run anything, and the same few lines are shown out of the many a real machine prints. Notice before you start that this connection is not called eth0: connection names vary from machine to machine, and that is ordinary rather than a fault. Find this machine's IPv4 address, and say which connection holds it.

content.title: The same reading, on a machine that looks different
paragraphs: That was PC-B. Its interface is called enp0s3 rather than eth0, its MAC address ends c2 rather than b7, and its IPv4 address is 192.168.1.11 rather than 192.168.1.10.

Nothing about the reading itself changed. You looked for four numbers separated by dots, and you looked at which connection name they sat beneath. The name of the connection was not the thing you were looking for — it was only where you looked.

That distinction is worth keeping. Connection names are not standardized across machines, so a reader who memorized eth0 is stuck the first time a machine disagrees. A reader who knows what shape of thing to look for is not.
That habit is what the mission is really for: saying what a machine actually holds, from its own report, is how you check a claim rather than trust it.

content.title: What the address does not tell you yet
paragraphs: You can now read PC-A's IPv4 address and PC-B's. Here is a question you still cannot answer from them: which other addresses does PC-A treat as sitting on its own network, reachable directly in the way you watched in Mission 2 — and which does it not?
192.168.1.11 is PC-B, and you might reasonably guess PC-A treats it as near. But guessing is not reading. What about 192.168.2.11? What about 10.0.0.5? Nothing you have looked at settles them.

So look again at what PC-A reported: inet 192.168.1.10/24. You accounted for the four numbers separated by dots. You did not account for everything on that line — a part after the address has said nothing to you yet, and it has been there since you first read it.
It is not an oversight in the output. It is what the machine itself uses to draw the line between near and far, and reading it is the whole of the next mission.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Two kinds of address on one interface: a MAC address used for local Ethernet delivery, and an IPv4 address assigned for IP. You can find both in the machine's own report.

What you cannot do yet is say where PC-A's own network ends. So far as you have read it, PC-A holds nothing that says which other addresses are close enough to reach the way Switch-1 delivered in Mission 2.
It does hold that, and you have already looked straight at it without being able to use it. So carry one question into the next mission: what tells the machine where its local network ends?

missions.title: Mission 4 — The prefix, and the decision every host makes
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a machine's assigned address from real output (Mission 3), and compare two numbers.

This is the mission the rest of the course rests on.

An assigned address is written with a second number after it. That number says how much of the address names the group the machine belongs to, and how much names the machine itself. A larger number means more of the address is fixed and the group is smaller. You will compare two of them so the number stops being decoration and starts being a quantity.

With that, a machine can answer the only question that matters before it sends anything: is what I am trying to reach part of my own group, or not? Watch a machine answer it both ways. When the answer is yes, it delivers directly, using what you learned in Mission 2 — and you will see the small exchange it performs first to learn the destination MAC address it needs for local delivery. When the answer is no, it does something you have not seen before: it hands the traffic to a different device entirely, one it was not trying to reach.

That hand-off will look wrong. Nothing was delivered to the destination, and yet nothing is broken. Deciding whether what you are watching is a fault or correct behavior is the most useful question in this course, and this is the first place you get to ask it with enough information to answer.

You will not be told what that other device is called yet. You will see what it receives and why, and the name comes next.

By the end you will be able to take two machines' addresses and say whether one will deliver to the other directly, and say what it does instead when it will not.

content.title: Two destinations, one machine
paragraphs: PC-A has two things to send, one after the other. One goes to a machine on its own network. One goes to a machine somewhere else entirely.
Your job: work out how PC-A tells those two situations apart, before anything moves.
PC-A holds 192.168.1.10, and PC-B holds 192.168.1.11. You read both off the machines in Mission 3.
The first is 192.168.1.11, which is PC-B. The second is 192.168.2.20, a machine called PC-C that you have not met.

Both are the same kind of address: four numbers separated by dots. Each of those four numbers is called an octet, so every IPv4 address has four octets. Nothing about how they are written says they are different sorts of thing.
PC-A does not treat them the same. Watch both, and the difference is what this mission is about. You have already seen the thing that explains it.

content.caption: PC-A reaching a destination inside its own group. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A network of five devices on one local network: PC-A, PC-B and a Printer, each with one interface, plus Switch-1 in the middle and Router-1 connected to Switch-1's fourth port. PC-A holds the address 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, PC-B holds 192.168.1.11 with 24 after it, and the Printer holds 192.168.1.12. Each interface also carries a MAC address of its own. The walkthrough follows PC-A being asked to reach 192.168.1.11. Before anything moves, PC-A asks itself one question: is that destination part of my own group? The 24 after its address is what answers it — it says the first three octets of the address name the group rather than the machine, so PC-A's group is 192.168.1. The destination 192.168.1.11 is also 192.168.1, so it is in the same group, and PC-A concludes it can deliver directly. It cannot deliver yet, though. Switch-1 does not use an IPv4 address like 192.168.1.11 to choose an outgoing port; it forwards local Ethernet traffic using destination MAC addresses. PC-A knows PC-B's IPv4 address but does not yet know PC-B's MAC address, so PC-A cannot yet build the local Ethernet frame for PC-B. So PC-A asks for it: a question addressed to no one in particular, saying whoever holds 192.168.1.11 should reply with their MAC address. That question arrives at Switch-1 on port 1, and Switch-1 sends a copy out of every other connection at the same moment — to PC-B, to the Printer and to Router-1. The Printer and Router-1 both compare the address against their own, find it is not theirs, and stay silent. PC-B recognizes the address as its own and answers with its MAC address, 00:1b:44:11:3a:c2. PC-A now holds both identities for the same machine, and the delivery proceeds: Switch-1 receives it on port 1, finds PC-B recorded against port 2, and sends it out of port 2 alone. It reached PC-B directly, and Router-1 was never involved.

nodes.label: PC-A

It reaches Switch-1 on port 1, and Switch-1 sends a copy out of every other connection at the same moment: to PC-B, to the Printer, and to Router-1.

stages.decision: Nothing has gone wrong at the two machines that stayed silent. Being asked a question that turns out not to be yours is ordinary: a machine compares the address against its own, finds it is not a match, and says nothing.

stages.narration: PC-A now has PC-B's IPv4 address and MAC address, and the delivery proceeds: Switch-1 receives the frame on port 1, finds PC-B's MAC address recorded on port 2, and forwards the frame through port 2 alone.
stages.decision: Nothing new happened in this last step. That is the point — the second half of this delivery is the ordinary local delivery you already know, unchanged. What this mission added is everything that had to happen before that delivery could begin.

confirmation.narration: It reached PC-B, directly, without Router-1 being involved at all.

Direct delivery still required PC-B's MAC address, so PC-A asked the local network and PC-B answered with that MAC address. After that, the frame followed the ordinary local-delivery behavior you already learned.

content.title: What PC-A was reading
paragraphs: The number after the address is called the prefix length. It is the answer to the question Mission 3 left you holding: what tells the machine where its own group ends.

It splits the address in two. The prefix length says how much of the address names the network — the group the machine belongs to — and what is left names the host, the individual machine inside that group. Those parts are the network portion and the host portion, and every address has both.

With /24 the split falls after the first three octets. In 192.168.1.10 the network portion is the first three octets, 192.168.1, and the host portion is the fourth, 10; in 192.168.1.11 it is 192.168.1 and 11. The network portions match, so the machines are on the same network — and that is the whole decision PC-A made before anything moved.

You are not calculating anything. You are reading two addresses, seeing which part of each names the network, and saying whether they match. That is the question a machine asks before everything it sends.

content.title: Turning one identity into the other
paragraphs: Deciding that the destination was local was not enough to deliver to it. Switch-1 forwards local Ethernet traffic using destination MAC addresses, so PC-A still needed PC-B's MAC address before it could send the frame.
So PC-A asked for it. The request it sent is called ARP. In this situation, ARP lets a host ask which MAC address is associated with a local IPv4 address.
Notice what ARP is not. It is not a lookup in a configured list or a service running somewhere else. It is a request sent on the local network, and the interface using that IPv4 address can answer.

This is where the two addresses connect. Mission 2 gave you the MAC address used for local Ethernet delivery; Mission 3 gave you the IPv4 address assigned to the interface. ARP supplies the local mapping PC-A needs before it can build the frame — and it works for this purpose on the local network, which is why PC-A settled the local question first.

content.title: Why everybody heard the question
paragraphs: Look again at how that question traveled. It arrived at Switch-1 on one port and left on every other one at the same moment — PC-B, the Printer and Router-1 all received it.

That is not the flooding you saw in Mission 2. Flooding was Switch-1 not knowing where a destination was, and it stopped as soon as it learned. This is PC-A addressing the question to everybody on purpose, because it could not address it to anybody in particular. That is called a broadcast.

The distinction is worth keeping straight, because the two look identical on the picture and mean opposite things. Flooding is a switch not knowing yet. A broadcast is a sender deciding that everyone should hear it.
Two machines received the question, compared the address against their own, found it was not theirs, and said nothing — the same behavior you watched the Printer perform in Mission 2.

content.title: The same question, a different destination
paragraphs: Now the second destination: 192.168.2.20.
Before you watch, work it out. PC-A's network portion is 192.168.1. Compare that against 192.168.2.20 and decide whether PC-A will treat this one the way it treated PC-B.
Then watch, and pay attention to what PC-A does NOT do, as much as to what it does.

content.caption: The same machine, asked to reach a destination outside its own group. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: The same local network as before — PC-A, PC-B, the Printer, Switch-1 and Router-1 — and beyond Router-1 a second machine, PC-C, holding the address 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it. PC-C is in a separate group of its own. The walkthrough follows PC-A being asked to reach 192.168.2.20. PC-A asks itself exactly the same question it asked before: is this destination part of my own group? It reads the same 24 after its own address, which says the first three octets name the group, so its group is still 192.168.1. The destination is 192.168.2, and that differing number sits inside the part that names the group, so the answer this time is no. PC-A therefore does not ask the network for 192.168.2.20's MAC address and does not attempt to deliver to it. Instead it hands what it is sending to Router-1, a device it was never trying to reach. Nothing was sent to PC-B or the Printer, and nothing arrived at 192.168.2.20 during the walkthrough. Nothing is broken. Why PC-A hands it to Router-1 in particular, and what Router-1 does with it afterwards, is not shown here.

content.title: Looks wrong, works as designed
paragraphs: PC-A was asked to reach 192.168.2.20 and sent what it was sending to Router-1, which is not 192.168.2.20 and never claimed to be. Nothing arrived at the destination in anything you watched.

In Mission 2 you were asked to form a habit: before deciding something is broken, ask whether it is the system working as designed. This is the second time that question has been worth asking, and this time you have enough to answer it.

It is working as designed. Everything PC-A can do by itself — ask for a local destination's MAC address and deliver a local frame — applies only on its own network. Delivering this remote traffic was never PC-A's job, and handing it to Router-1 is PC-A recognizing the limit of direct local delivery.
What PC-A did is settled. Why Router-1 is where it goes is not.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: You can now take two addresses, read which part of each names the network, say whether one machine will deliver to the other directly — and say what it does instead when it will not.
The prefix length is no longer decoration. It is the number a machine consults before everything it sends.

One thing was left standing. PC-A sent to Router-1 without hesitating and without asking anyone, so it was not working Router-1 out at the time — it already knew. Nothing you have looked at explains how, or why Router-1 rather than any other device.
So carry that into the next mission: how does PC-A know where to hand off, and why does it have to be that device in particular?

missions.title: Mission 5 — The default gateway
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: decide from two addresses whether a machine will deliver directly, and describe what it does instead when it will not (Mission 4).

In Mission 4 you watched a machine hand traffic to a device it was not trying to reach. That device has a name, and the machine did not guess at it — the address was configured in advance, and it is the machine's answer to "this is not for my group, so it is your problem now".

You will read that configuration from real output. There is one line in it that matters here, and you will learn to find that line and ignore the rest, which is a skill in itself.

Then you will work out why that address and not another. The device a machine hands traffic to has to be one the machine can reach directly, or the hand-off could never happen — which means it must be in the machine's own group. That single constraint explains almost every mistake people make with this setting, and you will meet one of those mistakes in Mission 8.

This is the smallest mission in the course, and deliberately so. It introduces one idea and one line of output. What that device actually does with the traffic once it has it is the next mission.

By the end you will be able to identify which address a machine will hand off to, and explain why that address has to be the one it is.

content.title: PC-A already knew
paragraphs: A workstation needs to reach another network, and it does not hesitate: it hands its traffic straight to one particular device without asking anything or anyone.
Your job: find the setting that told it to, and work out why it could not have been any other address.
That is what you watched at the end of Mission 4: PC-A worked out that 192.168.2.20 was not in its own group, then handed what it was sending to Router-1.
Look at how. It did not ask the network which device to use, and it did not try several. No pause, no search — PC-A turned to Router-1 the way you reach for something whose location you already know.
So PC-A already held the answer before the situation came up, which means somebody put it there in advance.
That is a fact about the machine, which means you can go and look. Read PC-A's configuration and find what told it where to send anything not local.

content.caption: PC-A's own configuration, as the machine reports it. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Two lines are shown, and only one of them can answer the question you are asking. Before you read on: work out which line tells PC-A where to send something that is NOT in its own group, and what the rest of each line is doing there.
content.output:
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto static metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.10

content.title: The line that answered it
paragraphs: It is the first one, and the part of it that matters is short: default via 192.168.1.1.

Read it plainly. By default — meaning when nothing more specific applies — send it via 192.168.1.1. That is a standing instruction, sitting on PC-A, waiting for exactly the situation Mission 4 produced.
Now look at the address itself. 192.168.1.1 is Router-1 — you could read it on Router-1's connection in Mission 4, where it sat unexplained. This is what it was for.

That standing instruction has a name: it is PC-A's default gateway. The setting holds one address, it is configured in advance rather than discovered, and it names the device a machine hands traffic to whenever the destination is not in its own group.

The second line describes PC-A's own group, and is not what you were looking for. Neither is proto static, metric 100, proto kernel or scope link. Real output is mostly not the answer to your question, and finding the line that is has more to do with knowing what you are looking for than with understanding every word on screen. You are not expected to know what all of those mean.

content.title: Why it has to be one of your own
paragraphs: Here is a question you can now answer without being told, using only what Mission 4 gave you. Could PC-A's default gateway have been 192.168.2.1 instead?

Work it through. PC-A holds 192.168.1.10/24, so its group is 192.168.1. Handing something to the gateway is itself a delivery, and PC-A only has one way of delivering: the way you watched in Mission 4, directly, inside its own group. It has no other method.

So if the configured address were 192.168.2.1, PC-A would have to reach 192.168.2.1 to hand anything over — and that is not in its group, so reaching it would require handing it to the gateway first. The machine would need the gateway in order to reach the gateway.

That is why the constraint exists: a machine's default gateway has to be an address the machine can already reach directly, which means it has to be in the machine's own group. 192.168.1.1 satisfies that. 192.168.2.1 could not.
Notice that you did not need a new rule for this. You used the one you already had, and it settled the question on its own. That is worth more than the setting itself.

content.title: What happens after the hand-off
paragraphs: That is the whole mission, and it is deliberately small. PC-A holds one configured address for everything not local; it is Router-1's, and it has to be something in PC-A's own group, because a hand-off is a local delivery like any other.
You can now say where a machine sends remote traffic, find that setting in real output, and explain why it could not have been just any address.
What you cannot say is what happens next. Router-1 holds something addressed to a machine it is not, in a group it is not in. PC-A's involvement has ended and the traffic has not arrived anywhere.
So carry this into the next mission: what does Router-1 actually do with it?

missions.title: Mission 6 — Routers, and the journey end to end
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: identify the device a machine hands off to and explain why it must be reachable directly (Mission 5).

Everything so far has been one half of a trip. Now you follow a whole one.

A message leaves a machine in one group, crosses to a device that belongs to two groups at once, and comes out the other side into a group it was never part of. Watch what changes at that device and what does not. The destination does not change — it was decided before the message left and it survives the whole trip. What wraps around it is thrown away and rebuilt at every step, because each step is a different local delivery of the kind you learned in Mission 2.

That distinction — the part that survives the journey and the part that is rebuilt for each leg — is the single most useful idea in this course, and it only makes sense once you have watched it happen. You have now watched local delivery twice and a hand-off once, so it is time.

Then the reply comes back, the same way in reverse, and you watch that too. A trip that only goes one way is not communication.

At the end of this mission, and not before, you get two labels. The decisions about reaching someone in your own group have a common name. The decisions about reaching another group have a different one. These are names for behavior you have already understood, not a framework to memorise. There are formal models that number these layers; you will meet them when you have a reason to, and this course does not give you one.

This mission introduces no new responsibility of its own. It puts five missions together into one continuous story, which is why nothing new is developed here and everything is used.

content.title: What Router-1 did with it
paragraphs: PC-A needs to reach PC-C, which is on another network. The traffic PC-A sent has now reached Router-1. That traffic is addressed to 192.168.2.20 — an address Router-1 does not hold, on a network the traffic did not arrive from. Router-1 has to decide where to send that traffic next.
Your job: follow that traffic across the network boundary, and watch PC-C's reply come back.
Mission 5 ended there. PC-A stopped being involved, and nothing had arrived anywhere.
That is the question you were asked to carry: what does Router-1 actually do with it?
You are about to watch the answer, and the reply coming back. Do not look for a new mechanism: everything in it is something you have already seen, arranged in an order you have not.
One thing to watch for: as it travels, some things stay the same the whole way and some are replaced at every step. Which is which is what this mission is for.

content.caption: One exchange between PC-A and PC-C, out and back, across two networks. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A network of six devices across two networks. On the first: PC-A holding 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, PC-B holding 192.168.1.11, a Printer holding 192.168.1.12, and Switch-1 connecting all three plus Router-1. On the second: PC-C holding 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it, connected directly to Router-1. Router-1 is the only device in both: its local connection holds 192.168.1.1 and its second connection holds 192.168.2.1. Each machine also carries a MAC address, the identity written on its interface. The walkthrough follows one exchange between PC-A and PC-C, out and back. PC-A has a packet for 192.168.2.20. Its own address is 192.168.1.10/24, and with a /24 prefix the first three octets name the network, so PC-A's network is 192.168.1.0/24 and the destination's is 192.168.2. A host delivers directly only inside its own network, so PC-A hands the packet to its default gateway, 192.168.1.1. The frame carrying it reaches Switch-1 on port 1, addressed to Router-1's MAC address 00:1b:44:11:3a:01; Switch-1 has never heard of 192.168.2.20, because that address is in the packet and a switch does not look there. Switch-1 forwards the frame out of port 4, and it arrives at Router-1's local connection. Router-1 sees that the destination 192.168.2.20 is not itself and not on the network it arrived from, but is on the network its second connection belongs to, so it builds a new frame and delivers the packet out of that connection — a second local delivery, on 192.168.2, addressed to PC-C's MAC address 00:1b:44:11:3a:e4. The frame that carried it across the first network ended at Router-1 and a new frame was built for the second. The packet inside never changed: 192.168.2.20 from beginning to end. PC-C then replies to 192.168.1.10, and performs the same reasoning in reverse: 192.168.1.10 is not in PC-C's group, so PC-C hands it to 192.168.2.1, Router-1's second connection. Router-1 receives it, finds 192.168.1.10 on its local connection's network, and delivers it there; Switch-1 carries it to port 1 and it arrives at PC-A. Four local deliveries on two networks, and four frames. On every leg the delivery was addressed to a MAC address on that leg's own network, and on no leg was that MAC address one of the two machines the exchange was actually between. Neither PC-A nor PC-C ever knew the other's MAC address, and neither needed to. Nothing reached PC-B or the Printer at any point.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the machine that started this exchange. PC-A holds 192.168.1.10/24, and PC-A has already compared 192.168.2.20 against its own network and found that address elsewhere. Everything PC-A can do by itself is already done.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is on this network and has nothing to do with this trip. It is here because it was here in Missions 2, 3 and 4, and because a network does not empty itself when one machine starts talking.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer, still on port 3, still uninvolved. Watch that nothing in this whole journey ever reaches it.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 delivers frames by MAC address, on this network only. Switch-1 has no idea that anything on this network is trying to reach another network, and nothing in this mission asks Switch-1 to know that.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 is the reason this trip is possible, and the reason is visible in Router-1's two interfaces rather than in anything clever Router-1 does. One connection holds an address on 192.168.1.0/24; the other holds an address on 192.168.2.0/24. Router-1 belongs to both networks at once, which no other device here does.

nodes.label: PC-C
nodes.about: PC-C is the machine PC-A is trying to reach. It holds 192.168.2.20/24, and like every machine you have met it holds one address to hand off to for anything outside its own network — which here is Router-1's other connection.

stages.action: deciding how to send the packet
stages.narration: PC-A has a packet for PC-C at 192.168.2.20. Its own address is 192.168.1.10/24, and the /24 means the first three octets name the network — so PC-A's network is 192.168.1.0/24. The destination's first three octets are 192.168.2, a different network. A host delivers directly only inside its own network, so PC-A hands the packet to its default gateway, 192.168.1.1.
stages.decision: Nothing here is new: PC-A compared two addresses and reached for the one it holds for everything outside its own network. What has never been shown is what happens on the other side of that hand-off, and that starts one step from now.

facts.label: Where it is trying to reach

stages.narration: The frame carrying the packet reaches Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 reads the destination MAC address on that frame: 00:1b:44:11:3a:01, which belongs to Router-1's local interface. PC-B and the Printer have received nothing.
stages.decision: Look at what Switch-1 is working from. Switch-1 is working from the frame's destination MAC address, and that MAC address belongs to Router-1. Switch-1 has never heard of 192.168.2.20, because that address is inside the packet and a switch does not look inside the packet. Two things are true at the same moment: the frame is going to Router-1, and the packet inside the frame is going to PC-C. Keeping those two apart is the whole of this mission.

stages.action: choosing which network to send it to
stages.narration: Switch-1 forwards the frame out of port 4, and it arrives at Router-1's local connection. Router-1 looks at the packet inside: it is going to 192.168.2.20, which is not Router-1, and not on the network the frame arrived from.
stages.decision: Router-1 is in a position no other device here is in. Its second connection holds 192.168.2.1, which is inside 192.168.2. The destination is inside 192.168.2. So the machine being looked for is reachable, directly, from Router-1's other side.

prediction.prompt: Router-1 is not 192.168.2.20, and 192.168.2.20 is not on the network this arrived from. Router-1's other connection holds 192.168.2.1. What does Router-1 do?
options: Sends it back to PC-A, because it is not the destination
Delivers it on its other connection, where that destination is local
Holds it until 192.168.2.20 asks for it

stages.narration: Router-1 builds a new frame for the second network and sends the packet out of its second connection, addressed to PC-C's MAC address, 00:1b:44:11:3a:e4. It arrives at PC-C.
stages.decision: The frame that carried the packet across the first network ended the moment the packet reached Router-1, and Router-1 built a new frame for the second network. What did not change is the packet: the packet was addressed to 192.168.2.20 before anything moved, and the packet is still addressed to 192.168.2.20 now.

stages.action: deciding how to send the reply
stages.narration: PC-C has the packet and replies. Watch PC-C do the same reasoning PC-A did: PC-C compares the reply's destination, 192.168.1.10, against its own address 192.168.2.20/24, finds a different network, and hands the reply to its own default gateway.
stages.decision: PC-C holds 192.168.2.20/24, so PC-C's network is 192.168.2.0/24. PC-C is replying to 192.168.1.10, which is on a different network. So PC-C will not deliver the reply directly either, and PC-C hands the reply to the one address it holds for everything outside its own network: 192.168.2.1, Router-1's second connection.

prediction.prompt: PC-C holds 192.168.2.20/24 and must reply to 192.168.1.10. Apply the same rule PC-A applied. What does PC-C do?
options: Delivers directly to 192.168.1.10, because it is a reply
Hands it to 192.168.2.1, because 192.168.1.10 is outside its group
Sends it to every machine on its network to find the way back

facts.label: Where it is trying to reach

stages.narration: The reply travels the first leg of its own trip: a local delivery on 192.168.2, addressed to Router-1's second connection, and it arrives there.
stages.decision: Same shape as the outbound first leg, on the other network. A new frame again, built for this leg and finished at the end of it.

stages.narration: Router-1 reads the reply's destination, 192.168.1.10, and finds that address on 192.168.1.0/24 — the network Router-1's local connection belongs to. So Router-1 delivers the reply onto that network, and Switch-1 carries the reply to port 1.
stages.decision: Router-1 did the same thing in both directions. Router-1 received a packet addressed to some other machine, found which of its two connections that destination sits behind, and made an ordinary local delivery on that connection's network.

stages.narration: It arrives at PC-A. The exchange PC-A started has now happened in both directions.
stages.decision: Four local deliveries, on two networks, carrying one exchange between two machines that were never on the same network. Neither PC-A nor PC-C ever knew the other's MAC address, and neither needed to.

confirmation.narration: It reached PC-C, and the reply reached PC-A. Two machines on different networks, and neither ever knew the other's MAC address.
confirmation.summary: One packet, four frames, two networks. Every delivery was made to a MAC address on that leg's own network — and on no leg was that MAC address the machine the exchange was actually between. What stayed the same from beginning to end was the packet and its destination, 192.168.2.20. What was built and finished four times, once per leg, was the frame that carried it across one network.

content.title: What survived, and what did not
paragraphs: Lay the four deliveries side by side. First leg: delivered to Router-1's MAC address, on 192.168.1. Second leg: delivered to PC-C's MAC address, on 192.168.2. Then the reply: to Router-1's other MAC address on 192.168.2, and finally to PC-A's on 192.168.1.
Four deliveries, four hardware identities, two networks. Not one was addressed to the machine the exchange was actually between — except at the last step, where PC-A happened to be both.

Now lay the destination beside those four deliveries. From the moment PC-A decided to send, the destination was 192.168.2.20. At Switch-1 the destination was still 192.168.2.20. At Router-1, still. On arrival at PC-C, still. PC-A chose that destination before anything moved, and no device along the way altered it.

Two things were true at once for the whole journey, doing different jobs. One said where this is ultimately for, and survived every step. The other said who hands this to whom right now, on this network, and was thrown away and rebuilt each leg. Every hard part of networking gets easier once those two stop being the same thing in your head.

content.title: The two units
paragraphs: You already have a name for the unit that gets rebuilt on every leg. Mission 2 called that unit a frame — and each of those four legs carried exactly one: a frame, built for one network, and finished at the far end of that network.

The unit inside each frame — the part addressed to 192.168.2.20, which kept that address the whole way — is the packet the journey named as you watched it. A packet is addressed to where the exchange is ultimately going, and a packet does not care how many networks lie between the sender and that destination.

So the relationship is simple, and you watched it rather than being told it: one packet traveled from PC-A to PC-C inside four different frames, because there were four local deliveries to make. The packet is the trip; a frame is one leg of it.

This is why Switch-1 could carry a packet addressed to 192.168.2.20 without any idea what that address is. Switch-1 was never looking at the packet — only at the frame around it, addressed to a MAC address, on Switch-1's own network.

content.title: What Router-1 was doing
paragraphs: Router-1 did the same thing twice, once in each direction, and it is worth saying plainly because it is less clever than it looks.

A packet arrived that was not addressed to Router-1, and was not going to a machine on the network the packet arrived from. Router-1 has two connections, each on a different network. Router-1 read the packet's destination, worked out which of its two connections that destination sits behind, and made an ordinary local delivery on that connection's network.
Deciding which way to send a packet that is not for you, so that it gets closer to where it is going, is called routing. That is the whole of what Router-1 contributed to this journey.

Notice what routing needed: a device belonging to more than one network at once, which is the only unusual thing about Router-1 and is visible in its two addresses. It did not need to understand the conversation or know anything about PC-A or PC-C.

content.title: Two kinds of decision
paragraphs: Every decision in this whole journey was one of exactly two kinds, and you can now sort them yourself.

Some were about getting something across one network, right now, to a MAC address on that network: Switch-1 delivering to a port, PC-A addressing its frame to Router-1, Router-1 addressing its frame to PC-C. Those decisions never look beyond the network they happen on. Collectively they are called Layer 2.

The others were about where this is ultimately going, and whether the destination is in my group or somewhere else: PC-A deciding 192.168.2.20 was remote, Router-1 deciding which connection sits closer to it, PC-C deciding the same in reverse. Those decisions ignore hardware identities entirely and work in assigned addresses. Collectively they are called Layer 3.

Treat those names as shorthand for behavior you have already watched, because that is all they are here. Formal models number these layers and add more; they are worth meeting when you have a reason to want them, and this course has not given you one. You have something more useful: you can look at a decision and say which kind it is.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Five missions came together into one trip: PC-A's local decision, the prefix that settled it, the hand-off address, the hardware identities the switch works from, and the topology you read in Mission 1. All of it in play, none of it new.
You can now follow an exchange from one network to another and back, and say at every step which identity is being used, which one survives, and which one is about to be replaced.

There is something you cannot do yet. Everything you just concluded, you concluded because you were shown it. In front of a real network nobody shows you that: the trip is not a picture, it either works or it does not, and you have to establish which from outside.
So carry this into the next mission: if nobody showed you, how would you find out whether any of that is actually happening?

missions.title: Mission 7 — Testing whether it actually works
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: follow a message from one group to another and back, and say what changes at each step (Mission 6).

So far you have been shown what happens. Now you find out for yourself.

There is a small test that asks a machine to answer, and reports whether it did. You will run it and read what comes back. Reading it is not the interesting part; deciding what to test is.

Here is the trap. A test that succeeds proves something specific, and it is almost never the thing people assume it proves. If a machine can reach the device it hands off to, that proves the first step works and says nothing about the rest of the trip. If it cannot reach that device, then nothing beyond it can possibly work, and testing anything further is wasted effort. Choosing what to test, in what order, so that each result actually narrows things down, is a different skill from running the test.

You will practice the difference between a result that confirms what you believe and a result that is merely consistent with it. Those feel identical in the moment and are not the same, and telling them apart is what separates someone who is checking from someone who is guessing.

By the end you will be able to choose which address to test in order to establish a specific claim, and say what a successful result does and does not prove.

content.title: Nobody draws it for you
paragraphs: Somebody asks you to confirm that PC-A really can reach PC-C. There is no drawing this time, nothing is animated, and nobody is going to show you the trip.
Your job: choose something to ask the network, and say exactly what the answer does and does not prove.
In Mission 6 you could say at every step which identity was being used and which survived. You knew all of it for one reason: the course showed you.
You believe the trip works. Now you have to establish it.
You cannot follow it. You cannot see the frames being rebuilt. Everything you understood was visible only because it was drawn for you, and none of it is visible now.

What you can do is ask. An answer you get from outside is something you observed rather than something you were told. So this mission is not about how to ask — it is about what an answer entitles you to conclude.

This is displayed output for you to read; nothing here offers to run anything, and no live network is involved. Before you read on, decide for yourself: this succeeded, so what does it prove?

content.title: What that actually proves
paragraphs: The tool is called ping. It asks one address to answer and reports whether it did, by sending a small message whose only purpose is to be replied to — a kind of message called ICMP, which exists for asking and answering questions about the network rather than carrying anything of your own. That is as much about ICMP as you need.
Now the part that matters. Three asks, three replies, nothing lost. Something answered from 192.168.1.1. Work out carefully what had to be true for that to happen.

PC-A had to build the ask and put it onto its own network. Switch-1 had to deliver it by hardware identity — so PC-A knew that identity, so Mission 4's exchange had already happened. Router-1 had to receive it and answer, and the answer had to come back. So the first leg — PC-A to Router-1 and back — works.

Here is what it does not give you. It says nothing about whether PC-C is reachable, nothing about whether Router-1 can deliver onto the other network, nothing about whether the far side is even switched on. It certainly does not establish that the network works — a result cannot be evidence about a path it did not take.

This is displayed output for you to read; nothing here offers to run anything, and no live network is involved. Before you read on: this also succeeded, so what does it let you conclude that the previous result did not?
content.output:
PING 192.168.2.20 (192.168.2.20) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.2.20: icmp_seq=1 ttl=63 time=1.284 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.2.20: icmp_seq=2 ttl=63 time=1.201 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.2.20: icmp_seq=3 ttl=63 time=1.233 ms
