content.title: Confirms, or merely consistent with
paragraphs: Something answered from 192.168.2.20, and that is a much larger result than the first one. For an answer to come back from there, the whole trip you watched in Mission 6 had to happen — out through Router-1 onto the other network, and back again. A reply cannot arrive unless the return path also worked. One successful answer from the far side establishes the round trip, for that address, at that moment.

Put the two results side by side, because the difference between them is the whole point of this mission. Both succeeded. Both look equally reassuring. They entitle you to completely different conclusions.

Suppose you believe the network is fine and you test 192.168.1.1. It answers. Does that confirm your belief? No — it is merely consistent with it. A working network produces that result; so does one where Router-1's far side is unplugged; so does one where PC-C has been off for a week. A result every one of those would produce cannot tell you which one you are in.

Now test 192.168.2.20 instead. It answers. That is not consistent with the far side being unplugged or PC-C being off, because neither could have produced a reply. It rules out the alternatives rather than merely fitting alongside them, which is what makes it evidence.

This is the habit worth taking away, and it costs nothing to apply: after any result, ask what else would have produced exactly the same thing. If the answer is "quite a lot", you have not learned as much as it feels like you have.

content.title: Choosing what to ask first
paragraphs: You now have two tests that establish different things, so you get to choose which to run — and the order is not arbitrary.
Consider a case you have not seen. Suppose PC-A could not reach 192.168.1.1 at all. Nothing answered. Before reading on, decide: would it be worth testing 192.168.2.20 next?

It would not, and the topology tells you why. Everything PC-A sends to the other network goes to Router-1 first. If PC-A cannot reach the one device it hands everything to, nothing beyond it can be reachable either — so that test would fail for a reason you already knew.

That is what makes a good first test. Not the one that answers the question you care about most, but the one whose result changes what you do next. A test that could only ever tell you something you already knew is not a diagnostic step, however easy it is to run.

So the ordering follows the path: ask about the nearest thing that has to work, and move outward once you know it does. Nothing is wrong here, and you are not being asked to find anything — you are learning to choose before there is pressure to choose well.

content.title: The question to carry forward
paragraphs: Everything you tested in this mission worked. Both asks were answered, and the only thing you had to be careful about was not claiming more than the answers supported.

You can now pick an address to ask about in order to establish one specific claim, and say afterwards what the result does and does not settle. That is a different skill from knowing how a network works, and it is the one that survives contact with a real one.
It has been easy so far because nothing has been wrong. Every result has agreed with what you expected, which means you have never had to act on one.
That changes next. Something is going to fail, and the reasoning you have just practiced is what turns a failure from a frustration into a starting point.

missions.title: Mission 8 — When it does not work
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: choose a test that establishes a specific claim, and say what its result proves (Mission 7).

A test that worked before now fails. Follow the evidence through the network, determine what the failure actually tells you, and use the stopping point to decide what to investigate next.

content.title: A result you have to act on
paragraphs: A user reports that PC-A cannot reach PC-C. Someone has already decided that the network is down. You do not know that yet, and neither do they.
PC-A is on 192.168.1.0/24. PC-C is on 192.168.2.0/24. Router-1 connects the two networks. That is the same topology you worked with in the previous missions.
Start with the evidence. Run the same connectivity check you used in Mission 7 and see what the result actually tells you.

content.caption: From PC-A, check whether PC-C at 192.168.2.20 answers. This is displayed output from the network; nothing here runs a live command. Before you read on, look at the result and decide what you can prove from it.
content.output:
PING 192.168.2.20 (192.168.2.20) 56(84) bytes of data.

--- 192.168.2.20 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 2043ms

content.title: A failure points in many directions
paragraphs: The result gives you one solid fact: PC-A did not receive a reply from 192.168.2.20.

It does not tell you why. PC-C could be unavailable. Router-1 might not be able to reach the second network. Something on PC-A could prevent the packet from leaving correctly. A connection somewhere along the path could also be unavailable. The failed ping looks the same from PC-A in each of those cases.
That is the difference between a failed test and a diagnosis. The test establishes what happened — no reply came back — but it does not identify which part of the path caused that result.

Mission 7 gave you a useful question: what else could have produced the same result? Here, several different problems could. To narrow them down, follow the packet from PC-A and find the last point where the evidence still shows normal delivery.

On a real network, troubleshooting can continue much further than this mission. That larger skill belongs to a later course. Here, your job is narrower: follow the evidence you are given, identify where delivery stops, and reason from that stopping point.

content.caption: Follow the packet from PC-A. At each step, use what the network shows you to decide whether delivery is still progressing normally or where it stops.
content.textEquivalent: A network of six devices across two networks. On the first: PC-A holding 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, PC-B holding 192.168.1.11, a Printer holding 192.168.1.12, and Switch-1 connecting all three plus Router-1. On the second: PC-C holding 192.168.2.20 with 24 after it, connected directly to Router-1. Router-1 is the only device in both networks: its local connection holds 192.168.1.1 and its second connection holds 192.168.2.1. One setting on PC-A is wrong. That setting is reported at each step as what PC-A is currently configured to hand off to, rather than listed among PC-A's fixed details, because it is the thing that changes. As found it is 192.168.2.1 rather than 192.168.1.1. The walkthrough begins with PC-A holding a packet for 192.168.2.20. PC-A's own address is 192.168.1.10/24, and with a /24 prefix the first three octets name the network, so PC-A's network is 192.168.1.0/24 and the destination's is 192.168.2. PC-A concludes correctly that the destination is on another network, so it reaches for the address it holds for anything outside its own, which is 192.168.2.1. The journey then stops at PC-A. Nothing leaves the machine, Switch-1 receives nothing, and no other device on either network sees anything. The visible facts at that stop are PC-A's own address 192.168.1.10 with 24 after it, the address it is configured to hand off to, 192.168.2.1, and that this address is not in PC-A's group. Three changes are offered. Setting PC-A to hand off to 192.168.1.1, Router-1's connection on PC-A's own network, is the one that restores the exchange: it is an address PC-A can reach directly, and it belongs to a device that is also in the destination's network. Setting PC-A to hand off to 192.168.1.12, the Printer, would make the hand-off itself possible but leaves the packet with a device that belongs to one network only. Giving Router-1 another address on PC-A's network changes nothing, because Router-1 already holds 192.168.1.1 and never received anything. After the correct change, PC-A is reported as currently configured to hand off to 192.168.1.1, and the journey continues: the frame reaches Switch-1 on port 1 and Switch-1 forwards it out of port 4 to Router-1's MAC address; Router-1 finds 192.168.2.20 on the network its second connection belongs to and delivers it there; it arrives at PC-C. PC-C answers 192.168.1.10, applies the same rule in reverse, hands the reply to 192.168.2.1, and Router-1 delivers it back onto PC-A's network, where Switch-1 carries it to port 1 and it arrives at PC-A, where PC-A is again reported as currently configured to hand off to 192.168.1.1. Nothing reached PC-B or the Printer at any point.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the machine that is trying to reach PC-C. What it holds and what it is wired to are here; the address it is currently configured to hand off to is a setting rather than a fixture, so it is reported beside each step as what PC-A is working from at that moment. Compare that address against PC-A's own network and see whether PC-A could reach it directly.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is on this network and is not involved. Nothing about PC-B has changed, and nothing in this journey reaches it.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is on PC-A's network, on port 3. It holds an address in 192.168.1, which means PC-A can reach it directly. It belongs to that one network and to no other.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 is unchanged and is working. Watch whether anything ever reaches it, because a device that receives nothing cannot be the device that failed.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 holds one address on each of its two connections, one for each network. It is the only device here that belongs to both. Nothing about Router-1 has been altered for this mission.

nodes.label: PC-C
nodes.about: PC-C is the machine PC-A is trying to reach. It holds 192.168.2.20, it is switched on, and its own settings are correct. Nothing has been changed here either.

stages.action: deciding how to send the packet
stages.narration: PC-A compares the destination against its own network before sending anything. PC-A's address is 192.168.1.10/24, and the /24 means the first three octets name the network — so PC-A is on 192.168.1.0/24. The destination 192.168.2.20 begins 192.168.2, which is a different network. A host delivers a packet directly only inside its own network, so PC-A hands this packet to its default gateway instead.
stages.decision: Every part of that reasoning is correct, and it is worth being sure of before anything goes wrong. PC-A compared the two networks properly and reached for the setting that exists for exactly this case. Whatever fails next, it does not fail here.

facts.label: Where it is trying to reach

prediction.prompt: PC-A has a packet addressed to PC-C at 192.168.2.20. PC-A's own address is 192.168.1.10/24. What does PC-A do first?
options: PC-A sends the packet straight to 192.168.2.20, because that is the address it was given
PC-A compares 192.168.2.20 against its own network to decide whether PC-C is local or remote
PC-A sends the packet to every device on its own network so that PC-C can claim it
prediction.correctOption: PC-A compares 192.168.2.20 against its own network to decide whether PC-C is local or remote

stages.narration: The packet never leaves PC-A. Switch-1 receives nothing, so no other device on either network sees the packet at all.

facts.label: Currently configured to hand off to

knowledgeChecks.prompt: The packet never left PC-A. Switch-1, Router-1 and PC-C each received nothing. What does that result allow you to conclude?
options: PC-C is switched off, which is why nothing came back
Router-1 failed to forward the packet to the second network
The packet never left PC-A, so the investigation stays at PC-A
Switch-1 discarded the packet instead of forwarding it
knowledgeChecks.correctOption: The packet never left PC-A, so the investigation stays at PC-A
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A device can only mishandle a packet it was given. Switch-1, Router-1 and PC-C were given nothing, so none of them can be the device that failed. That rules out three of the four suspects at once and leaves the failure at PC-A, before the packet reached the wire.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: PC-A decided correctly that PC-C is on another network, and then could not send the packet. What should you inspect next?
options: PC-C's power state
Router-1's second connection
The address PC-A is configured to hand off to
Switch-1's record of which device is on which port
knowledgeChecks.correctOption: The address PC-A is configured to hand off to
knowledgeChecks.explanation: PC-A got as far as choosing to use its default gateway and then stopped. The next thing PC-A had to act on is the gateway address it was configured with, so that address is the next thing to look at.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.1.10/24 and is configured to hand off to 192.168.2.1. Can PC-A deliver a packet directly to that gateway address?
options: Yes — a default gateway is always reachable by definition
Yes — 192.168.2.1 belongs to Router-1, and PC-A is connected to Router-1
No — 192.168.2.1 is not on 192.168.1.0/24, so reaching it would itself need a gateway
knowledgeChecks.correctOption: No — 192.168.2.1 is not on 192.168.1.0/24, so reaching it would itself need a gateway
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Handing a packet to a gateway is itself a local delivery, and a host can deliver directly only inside its own network. PC-A's network is 192.168.1.0/24, and 192.168.2.1 begins 192.168.2, so PC-A cannot reach that address directly. To reach its gateway PC-A would first need a gateway, which is the very thing it is trying to do. A gateway a host cannot reach directly is a gateway that host cannot use.

stages.narration: Now it leaves. The frame reaches Switch-1 on port 1, and Switch-1 forwards it out of port 4 to Router-1's MAC address, on this network. PC-B and the Printer see nothing.
stages.decision: Nothing about Switch-1 changed. It was working before the repair and it is working now; it simply had nothing to carry.

deviceFacts.label: What PC-A is working from now

facts.label: Currently configured to hand off to

stages.narration: Switch-1 forwards the frame out of port 4, and it arrives at Router-1's local connection. Router-1 finds 192.168.2.20 on the network its second connection belongs to, builds a new frame for that network, and delivers the packet to PC-C's MAC address.
The packet reaches PC-C — the first thing to arrive anywhere in this mission.
PC-C answers 192.168.1.10, applies the same rule in reverse, and hands its reply to 192.168.2.1. Router-1 receives it and finds 192.168.1.10 on its local connection's network.
Router-1 delivers the reply onto PC-A's network, and Switch-1 carries it towards port 1.
The reply reaches PC-A. The packet left, arrived at PC-C, was answered, and the answer came back.
stages.decision: This is the part that turns a change into a repair. You did not merely alter a setting and assume it helped — you watched the thing that was failing succeed, end to end, and come back.

deviceFacts.label: What PC-A is working from now

facts.label: Currently configured to hand off to

fault.symptom: PC-A could not deliver the packet to the gateway address it is configured to use.
fault.explanation: PC-A is 192.168.1.10/24, so PC-A's own network is 192.168.1.0/24. The configured gateway, 192.168.2.1, is on a different network, and handing a packet to a gateway is itself a local delivery. PC-A would need a gateway in order to reach its gateway, so the packet has nowhere to go and never reaches the wire. A gateway a host cannot reach directly is a gateway that host cannot use.

actions.label: Set PC-A's gateway to 192.168.1.1 — Router-1's interface on PC-A's own network
actions.observation: Correct, and both halves of the reason matter. PC-A can deliver to 192.168.1.1 directly, because that address is on 192.168.1.0/24 with PC-A — so the hand-off is a delivery PC-A can actually make. And Router-1 also holds an address on the destination's network, 192.168.2.1, so once Router-1 has the packet there is somewhere for the packet to go. A gateway has to be reachable AND has to be on both networks.

actions.label: Set PC-A's gateway to 192.168.1.12 — the Printer, which PC-A can reach directly
actions.observation: Half right, and the half that is right is the half most people get wrong — so this is worth being clear about. PC-A CAN reach 192.168.1.12 directly, because the Printer is on 192.168.1.0/24 with PC-A. The hand-off that just failed would now succeed. But being reachable is only what PC-A needs from a gateway. The gateway also has to be able to forward the packet onward, and the Printer holds an address on this network and on no other — so a packet addressed to 192.168.2.20 arrives somewhere with nowhere to send it. Reachable is necessary. It is not sufficient. Choose again.

actions.label: Set PC-A's gateway to 192.168.2.20 — PC-C, the machine PC-A is trying to reach
actions.observation: This is the same mistake the network already has, aimed at a different address. 192.168.2.20 begins 192.168.2, so it is not on PC-A's network — and PC-A cannot deliver directly to an address off its own network, which is exactly why the packet stopped. A gateway is not where the packet is going. It is the device PC-A hands the packet TO, on the way, and PC-A has to be able to reach it directly. Choose again.

actions.label: Change the destination to 192.168.1.12 — the Printer, which PC-A can reach
actions.observation: That does make a packet leave PC-A, and it repairs nothing. The user needs to reach PC-C at 192.168.2.20; sending to the Printer instead is a different exchange that happens to succeed. The evidence pointed at one setting on one machine — the gateway PC-A could not reach. Changing the destination leaves that setting exactly as broken as it was, and the next packet for another network will stop in the same place. Change the thing the evidence indicated. Choose again.

confirmation.narration: It reached PC-C, and the reply reached PC-A. The thing that was failing is now working, and you watched it work rather than assuming it.
confirmation.summary: One setting was wrong, on one machine, and nothing else on either network had been touched. The stop told you where to look: PC-A had decided correctly and then been unable to act, which pointed at what PC-A was configured to act on rather than at anything further along. Changing it was the repair. Watching the whole exchange complete, out and back, is what makes it a repair rather than a hope.

content.title: Working backwards from the stop
paragraphs: A stopping point is worth two readings, and most of the value is in the one people skip. The first is what was still working. PC-A compared 192.168.2.20 against its own network, concluded that PC-C was somewhere else, and reached for the address it keeps for exactly that case. Every part of that reasoning was correct. Whatever was wrong, PC-A's local-versus-remote decision was not — and the stop is what proved that decision was working.

The second reading is what the stop rules out, and the stop rules out a great deal at once. Switch-1, Router-1 and PC-C received nothing, and a device that received nothing cannot be the device that failed. Three of your four suspects are gone. The failure was at PC-A, before the packet reached the wire, and PC-A had only one thing left to be wrong about: the gateway address it had been configured with.

That is the conclusion you reached at the stop, and it is worth naming: 192.168.2.1 is a real address on a real device, and it is not an address PC-A can reach. Mission 5 worked that constraint out on paper. This is what the constraint looks like when a machine is actually configured that way.
Correcting the fault took one value, on one machine, chosen because the evidence pointed there. That is what makes a repair bounded: you changed the thing the evidence indicated, and nothing else.

content.title: A repair you did not confirm is a hope
paragraphs: You then watched the whole exchange complete — out through Switch-1 to Router-1, across to PC-C, and back to PC-A with a reply. It is tempting to treat that as a formality. It is the opposite.

"I changed the setting" and "the thing that was failing now works" are two different claims, and only the second is what anybody wanted. Changing a setting is something you did. Working is something you have to observe. A repair you did not confirm is a claim about behavior with no observation behind it.

The confirmation is also bounded, in exactly the way Mission 7 described. The reply that came back establishes that this exchange, to this address, worked at that moment. The reply does not establish that nothing else on either network is wrong, and no single test could. A confirmed repair is a settled question, not a healthy network.
Symptom, evidence, one bounded change, confirmation. The networks get larger and the settings get stranger; that shape does not change.

content.title: What you have, and what you have not, shown
paragraphs: That was the last mission, so it is worth being accurate about where you have arrived.

You started with a network you had no vocabulary for. You can now read a topology, follow a frame inside one network, read the two identities an interface carries, decide whether a destination is local or remote, say why a host needs a gateway and what makes an address eligible to be one, follow a packet across a network boundary and back, choose a test that establishes one specific claim, and take a bounded failure from symptom to a correction you confirmed.

Be equally accurate about the other side. You have been taught these things; you have not yet demonstrated them. The journeys were drawn for you, the results were shown to you, and the one failure you met had already been located before you arrived. Reading a stopping point somebody else found is a genuine skill, and a smaller one than finding a failure nobody has located.

So this course does not tell you that you are ready for anything in particular, and you should be wary of any course that would. What it has given you is better than a claim: a model that holds together. The pieces connect, nothing was simplified into something you will later have to unlearn, and you can say why each part is true rather than only that it is.
When you started, a network was a box of wires and a diagram you could not read. It is not that any more. What comes next is doing this somewhere nobody has drawn it for you.

competencies.title: Network topology literacy
competencies.description: Identify the hosts, switches and routers in a network topology, name the interfaces and ports that connect them, and state which device is responsible for each part of a path between two machines.

competencies.title: Local network delivery
competencies.description: Explain how a switch delivers traffic to one host within a single network, how it learns where hosts are, what it does with a destination it has not learned, and why traffic for another network is handed elsewhere.

competencies.title: IPv4 address identification
competencies.description: Identify the IPv4 address assigned to a host's interface, read it from device or operating-system output, and distinguish an assigned address from the interface's built-in hardware identity.

competencies.title: IPv4 addressing
competencies.description: Assign and interpret an IPv4 address and prefix length, and determine which addresses a host can reach without assistance from a router.

competencies.title: Subnet boundaries
competencies.description: Determine from an address and prefix length whether two hosts share a subnet, and recognise the boundary at which forwarding becomes a router's responsibility.

competencies.title: Default gateway relationships
competencies.description: Identify the correct default gateway for a host and explain why off-subnet traffic depends on it.

competencies.title: Connectivity verification
competencies.description: Choose verification steps that establish what actually works, and distinguish a test that confirms a hypothesis from one merely consistent with it.
